qs.q:
Consider the matrices
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}-8&-4\\23&12\\18&10\end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}-2&9\end{bmatrix}$$
What are the sizes (rows × columns) of $A$ and $B$?
e: The size of a matrix is $M \times N$, where $M$ is the number of rows and $N$ is the number of columns.
$A$ has 3 rows and 2 columns, so its size is $3 \times 2$.
$B$ has 1 row and 2 columns, so its size is $1 \times 2$.
<mark>$A$ is $3 \times 2$ and $B$ is $1 \times 2$.</mark>

qs.q:
Let
$$B = \begin{bmatrix}4&14&-7\\18&5&13\\-20&4&22\end{bmatrix}$$
What are the elements $b_{21}$ and $b_{13}$?
e: The element $b_{ij}$ is located in row $i$ and column $j$ (the row number comes first).
$b_{21}$ is in row 2, column 1, so $b_{21} = 18$.
$b_{13}$ is in row 1, column 3, so $b_{13} = -7$.

qs.q:
Let
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}-7&\sqrt{16}&13\\\frac{1}{2}&2&8\end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}-7&4&13\\0.5&2&8\end{bmatrix}$$
Is $A = B$?

c.x: No, because $\sqrt{16}$ is not written in the same form as $4$
No, because $\frac{1}{2}$ is not written in the same form as $0.5$
Yes, but only because both matrices have the same size
Yes, because the sizes are equal and corresponding elements are equal

e: Two matrices are equal when (1) they have the same size and (2) $a_{ij} = b_{ij}$ for all corresponding elements.
Both matrices are $2 \times 3$, so the first condition holds.
Compare the elements by value: $\sqrt{16} = 4$ and $\frac{1}{2} = 0.5$, and all other entries are identical.
<mark>Both conditions hold, so $A = B$.</mark>

qs.q:
Using equal matrices, find $x$ and $y$ if
$$\begin{bmatrix}3&4\\-7&4\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}x&y+2\\-7&4\end{bmatrix}$$
e: Equal matrices have equal corresponding elements.
Position $(1,1)$: $x = 3$.
The remaining entries $-7$ and $4$ already match.
<mark>$x = 3$ and $y = 2$</mark>

qs.q:
Let
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}4&5&2\\-3&6&0\end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}0&3&-5\\4&-5&7\end{bmatrix}$$
What is $A - B$?
e: Both matrices are $2 \times 3$, so subtraction is defined. Subtract corresponding elements.
<mark>$A - B = \begin{bmatrix}4&2&7\\-7&11&-7\end{bmatrix}$</mark>

qs.q: Let $A$ and $B$ be $2 \times 3$ matrices and let $C$ be a $2 \times 2$ matrix. Which of the following expressions is <u>defined</u>?
e: Addition and subtraction require both matrices to have the <u>same size</u>.
$A$ and $C$ have sizes $2 \times 3$ and $2 \times 2$, so $A - C$ is undefined. The same holds for $B + C$ and $C - B$.
$A$ and $B$ are both $2 \times 3$.
<mark>Only $A + B$ is defined.</mark>

qs.q: For two matrices $A$ and $B$ of the same size, which statement is correct?

c.x: $A + B = B + A$ and $A - B = B - A$ always hold
$A + B \neq B + A$ and $A - B \neq B - A$ in general
$A + B = B + A$, but $A - B \neq B - A$ in general
$A + B \neq B + A$, but $A - B = B - A$ in general

e: Addition is done element by element, and $a_{ij} + b_{ij} = b_{ij} + a_{ij}$, so $A + B = B + A$.
Subtraction is not commutative: $a_{ij} - b_{ij}$ is generally different from $b_{ij} - a_{ij}$ (it has the opposite sign).
<mark>$A + B = B + A$, but $A - B \neq B - A$ in general.</mark>

qs.q:
Let
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}2&3&4\\1&3&1\end{bmatrix},\quad B = \begin{bmatrix}0&2&7\\-1&3&-5\end{bmatrix},\quad C = \begin{bmatrix}9&-6&3\\3&0&12\end{bmatrix}$$
Find $2A - B + \frac{1}{3}C$.
e: Multiply each matrix by its scalar: $2A = \begin{bmatrix}4&6&8\\2&6&2\end{bmatrix}$.
$(-1)B = \begin{bmatrix}0&-2&-7\\1&-3&5\end{bmatrix}$.
$\frac{1}{3}C = \begin{bmatrix}3&-2&1\\1&0&4\end{bmatrix}$.
Add the three matrices element by element. Row 1: $4 + 0 + 3 = 7$, $\;6 - 2 - 2 = 2$, $\;8 - 7 + 1 = 2$.
<mark>$2A - B + \frac{1}{3}C = \begin{bmatrix}7&2&2\\4&3&11\end{bmatrix}$</mark>

qs.q: Let $A$ be a $2 \times 3$ matrix and $B$ be a $3 \times 4$ matrix. Which statement is correct?

c.x: $AB$ is defined and its size is $2 \times 4$
$BA$ is defined and its size is $4 \times 2$
$AB$ is defined and its size is $3 \times 3$
$AB$ is defined and its size is $3 \times 4$

e: $AB$ is defined only if the number of columns of $A$ equals the number of rows of $B$.
Columns of $A = 3$ and rows of $B = 3$, so $AB$ is defined.
The size of $AB$ is (rows of $A$) × (columns of $B$) $= 2 \times 4$.
For $BA$: columns of $B = 4$ but rows of $A = 2$, so $BA$ is <u>not</u> defined.
<mark>$AB$ is defined and is $2 \times 4$.</mark>

qs.q:
Find $AB$ for
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2&4\\2&6&0\end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}4&1&4&3\\0&-1&3&1\\2&7&5&2\end{bmatrix}$$
e: $A$ is $2 \times 3$ and $B$ is $3 \times 4$, so $AB$ is defined and has size $2 \times 4$.
Each entry is (row of $A$) · (column of $B$). Row 1 of $A$ is $[1\;\;2\;\;4]$:
<mark>$AB = \begin{bmatrix}12&27&30&13\\8&-4&26&12\end{bmatrix}$</mark>

qs.q: Suppose the sizes are $A(4 \times 5)$, $B(4 \times 5)$, $C(5 \times 2)$, $D(4 \times 2)$, $E(5 \times 4)$. How many of the following four expressions are defined? $$BA, \qquad AC + D, \qquad AE + B, \qquad E(A + B)$$
e: $BA$: $B$ is $4 \times 5$ and $A$ is $4 \times 5$. Columns of $B = 5 \neq 4 =$ rows of $A$, so it is <u>undefined</u>.
$AC + D$: $AC$ is $(4 \times 5)(5 \times 2) = 4 \times 2$, and $D$ is $4 \times 2$, so the sum is defined.
$AE + B$: $AE$ is $(4 \times 5)(5 \times 4) = 4 \times 4$, but $B$ is $4 \times 5$, so the sum is <u>undefined</u>.
$E(A + B)$: $A + B$ is $4 \times 5$, and $E(A+B)$ is $(5 \times 4)(4 \times 5) = 5 \times 5$, so it is defined.
<mark>Exactly 2 expressions are defined: $AC + D$ and $E(A + B)$.</mark>

qs.q: Suppose $A$ and $B$ are both $4 \times 5$ matrices and $E$ is a $5 \times 4$ matrix. What is the size of $E(A + B)$?
e: First, $A + B$ is defined because $A$ and $B$ have the same size, and its size is $4 \times 5$.
Now multiply $E$ ($5 \times 4$) by $(A + B)$ ($4 \times 5$). The inner dimensions match ($4 = 4$).
The size of the product is (rows of $E$) × (columns of $A + B$) $= 5 \times 5$.
<mark>$E(A + B)$ is $5 \times 5$.</mark>

qs.q:
Let
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$$
Which statement is correct?
e: Compute $AB$: row 1 of $A$ is $[1\;\;2]$, and the columns of $B$ are $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$. Entries: $1\cdot0+2\cdot1 = 2$ and $1\cdot1+2\cdot0 = 1$.
Row 2 of $A$ is $[0\;\;1]$: $0\cdot0+1\cdot1 = 1$ and $0\cdot1+1\cdot0 = 0$. So $AB = \begin{bmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}$.
Compute $BA$: row 1 of $B$ is $[0\;\;1]$, and the columns of $A$ are $(1,0)$ and $(2,1)$. Entries: $0\cdot1+1\cdot0 = 0$ and $0\cdot2+1\cdot1 = 1$.
Row 2 of $B$ is $[1\;\;0]$: $1\cdot1+0\cdot0 = 1$ and $1\cdot2+0\cdot1 = 2$. So $BA = \begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{bmatrix}$.
<mark>$AB \neq BA$: matrix multiplication is not commutative.</mark>

qs.q: Which of the following matrices is a diagonal matrix?
e: A diagonal matrix is a <u>square</u> matrix in which all entries that are not on the main diagonal are zero.
$\begin{bmatrix}4&3\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ has the nonzero entry $3$ off the main diagonal.
The $3 \times 3$ matrix with entries $4, 3, -7, 6, 5, -2$ off the diagonal has several nonzero off-diagonal entries.
$\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&2&0\end{bmatrix}$ is $2 \times 3$, so it is not square.
The $4 \times 4$ matrix is square and every off-diagonal entry is $0$ (zeros on the main diagonal are allowed).
<mark>The $4 \times 4$ matrix is diagonal.</mark>

qs.q: Which statement about the identity matrix $I$ and diagonal matrices is correct?

c.x: Every diagonal matrix is an identity matrix
Every identity matrix is diagonal, but not every diagonal matrix is an identity matrix
Every identity matrix is square, but no identity matrix is diagonal
Identity matrices and diagonal matrices are exactly the same set

e: The identity matrix is a diagonal matrix whose main diagonal entries are all equal to $1$.
So every identity matrix is diagonal.
The converse is false: for example $\begin{bmatrix}6&0\\0&7\end{bmatrix}$ is diagonal but its diagonal entries are not all $1$.
<mark>Every identity matrix is diagonal, but not every diagonal matrix is an identity matrix.</mark>

qs.q: Let $A$ be a $2 \times 3$ matrix. Which identity matrices make $IA = A$ and $AI = A$, respectively?
e: For $IA$ to be defined, the columns of $I$ must equal the rows of $A$, which is $2$. So $I = I_2$, and then $I_2 A$ is $2 \times 3$.
For $AI$ to be defined, the rows of $I$ must equal the columns of $A$, which is $3$. So $I = I_3$, and then $A I_3$ is $2 \times 3$.
<mark>$I_2$ is used for $IA = A$ and $I_3$ is used for $AI = A$.</mark>

qs.q: How is the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}1&-9&-3\end{bmatrix}$ classified?
e: A vector matrix has only one row or only one column.
This matrix has 1 row and 3 columns, so it is a row vector of size $1 \times 3$.
It is not a zero matrix, because its entries are not all zero.
<mark>It is a row vector of size $1 \times 3$.</mark>

qs.q: Let $O$ be the zero matrix of the same size as a matrix $A$. Which statement is correct?

c.x: $A + O = O + A = A - O = A$

e: Adding or subtracting $0$ from each element does not change the element.
So $A + O = A$, $\;O + A = A$, and $A - O = A$.
<mark>$A + O = O + A = A - O = A$</mark>

qs.q:
Let
$$B = \begin{bmatrix}2&3\\1&4\\5&6\end{bmatrix}$$
What is $B^T$?
e: $B$ is $3 \times 2$, so $B^T$ is $2 \times 3$.
The rows of $B$ become the columns of $B^T$.
Row 1 of $B$ is $[2\;\;3]$, so column 1 of $B^T$ is $(2, 3)$. Row 2 is $[1\;\;4]$, so column 2 is $(1, 4)$. Row 3 is $[5\;\;6]$, so column 3 is $(5, 6)$.
<mark>$B^T = \begin{bmatrix}2&1&5\\3&4&6\end{bmatrix}$</mark>

qs.q: Let $A$ be a $2 \times 3$ matrix and $B$ be a $3 \times 4$ matrix. Which expression equals $(AB)^T$?
e: The transpose rule for products is $(AB)^T = B^T A^T$ (the order is reversed).
Check the sizes: $B^T$ is $4 \times 3$ and $A^T$ is $3 \times 2$, so $B^T A^T$ is defined and is $4 \times 2$, which matches the size of $(AB)^T$ (since $AB$ is $2 \times 4$).
$A^T B^T$ is $(3 \times 2)(4 \times 3)$, which is undefined. The same problem occurs with $AB^T$ and $BA$.
<mark>$(AB)^T = B^T A^T$</mark>

qs.q: Which of the following matrices is symmetric?
e: A square matrix is symmetric when $A = A^T$, i.e. $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all entries.
Option 1: $a_{12} = -3$ but $a_{21} = 3$, so it is not symmetric.
Option 2: $a_{23} = -2$ but $a_{32} = 2$, so it is not symmetric.
Option 3: $a_{13} = 1$ but $a_{31} = 0$, so it is not symmetric.
<mark>Option 4 is symmetric.</mark>

qs.q:
Let
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\1&3\end{bmatrix}, \qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}3&-2\\-1&1\end{bmatrix}$$
Is $B$ the inverse of $A$?

c.x: No, because $A$ and $B$ do not have the same size

e: Square matrices $A$ and $B$ of the same size satisfy $B = A^{-1}$ when $AB = BA = I$.
$AB$: $\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot3+2\cdot(-1)&1\cdot(-2)+2\cdot1\\1\cdot3+3\cdot(-1)&1\cdot(-2)+3\cdot1\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix} = I$.
$BA$: $\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot1+(-2)\cdot1&3\cdot2+(-2)\cdot3\\-1\cdot1+1\cdot1&-1\cdot2+1\cdot3\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix} = I$.
<mark>$AB = BA = I$, so $B$ is the inverse of $A$.</mark>

qs.q:
Using the $2 \times 2$ inverse formula, find $A^{-1}$ for
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}1&4\\2&7\end{bmatrix}$$
e: For $A = \begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}$, the inverse is $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}$.
Here $a = 1$, $b = 4$, $c = 2$, $d = 7$, so $ad - bc = 1\cdot7 - 4\cdot2 = -1$ (nonzero, so $A$ is invertible).
Swap $a$ and $d$, and change the signs of $b$ and $c$: $\begin{bmatrix}7&-4\\-2&1\end{bmatrix}$.
Multiply by $\frac{1}{-1} = -1$: $A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}-7&4\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}$.
<mark>$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}-7&4\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}$</mark>

qs.q:
Let
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}3&6\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$$
Which statement about $A$ is correct?

c.x: $ad - bc = 0$, so its inverse is the zero matrix
$ad - bc = 0$, so $A$ is singular (it has no inverse)

e: If $ad - bc = 0$, the matrix has no inverse (it is singular). The formula would require dividing by $0$.
<mark>$A$ is singular (not invertible).</mark>

qs.q:
To find $A^{-1}$ in Example 1, we reduce $[A \mid I]$. After $-2R_1 + R_2 \to R_2$ and $-3R_1 + R_3 \to R_3$ we get
$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&2&3&1&0&0\\0&0&-1&-2&1&0\\0&-1&-3&-3&0&1\end{array}\right]$$
Which operation should be applied next?
e: The next leading 1 should be in column 2, row 2, but the entry in row 2, column 2 is $0$.
Multiplying $R_2$ by $-1$ keeps that entry equal to $0$, and adding $R_2$ to $R_1$ does not change row 2.
$R_3$ has a nonzero entry ($-1$) in column 2, so interchange $R_2$ with $R_3$.
<mark>Interchange $R_2$ with $R_3$.</mark>

qs.q:
Find $A^{-1}$ for
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2&3\\2&4&5\\3&5&6\end{bmatrix}$$
e: Form $[A \mid I]$ and reduce the left half to $I$.
The right half is now $A^{-1}$.
<mark>$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}1&-3&2\\-3&3&-1\\2&-1&0\end{bmatrix}$</mark>

qs.q:
To show that
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}1&6&4\\2&4&-1\\-1&2&5\end{bmatrix}$$
is not invertible, we reduce $[A \mid I]$ and obtain
$$\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1&6&4&1&0&0\\0&1&\frac{9}{8}&\frac{1}{4}&-\frac{1}{8}&0\\0&0&0&-1&1&1\end{array}\right]$$
Which observation proves that $A$ is not invertible?

c.x: The left half has a zero row, so it cannot be reduced to $I$
The right half contains fractions such as $\frac{1}{4}$ and $-\frac{1}{8}$
The right half has a nonzero third row, which is not allowed
The left half has the entry $\frac{9}{8}$, which is not an integer

e: $A$ is invertible only if $[A \mid I]$ can be reduced to $[I \mid A^{-1}]$.
Here the third row of the left half is $[0\;\;0\;\;0]$ (it came from $-8R_2 + R_3 \to R_3$).
A zero row in the left half means the left half can never become the identity matrix.
Fractions in the matrix are allowed during row operations, and a nonzero right half does not prevent invertibility by itself.
<mark>The zero row in the left half shows that $A$ is not invertible.</mark>

qs.q: Let $A$ and $B$ be invertible matrices of the same size. Which expression equals $(AB)^{-1}$?
e: For invertible matrices of the same size, $AB$ is invertible and $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$ (the order is reversed).

qs.q:
Let $A$ be an invertible matrix with
$$A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}-7&4\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}$$
What is $(2A)^{-1}$?
e: The property is $(KA)^{-1} = \frac{1}{K}A^{-1}$ for a nonzero constant $K$.
Multiply every element of $A^{-1}$ by $\frac{1}{2}$: $-7 \to -\frac{7}{2}$, $\;4 \to 2$, $\;2 \to 1$, $\;-1 \to -\frac{1}{2}$.
<mark>$(2A)^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix}-\frac{7}{2}&2\\1&-\frac{1}{2}\end{bmatrix}$</mark>

qs.q: Let $A$ and $B$ be square matrices of the same size, and suppose the product $AB$ is <u>not</u> invertible. Which statement must be true?
e: If $A$ and $B$ were both invertible, then $AB$ would be invertible, with $(AB)^{-1} = B^{-1}A^{-1}$.
Since $AB$ is not invertible, at least one of the two matrices must be non-invertible. It is not required that both are.
<mark>$A$ or $B$ is not invertible.</mark>
